lesson.subtitle: Lesson 36 — A Place You Can See
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 36 — A Place You Can See
lesson.grammar_point: relative clauses for describing places (where / which / whose)

listenings.text: Have you noticed that some people describe places so well that you can almost see them? Their secret is simple. They don't start with big words like beautiful or nice. They start with one small, real detail. Not, my city is beautiful, but, my city is a place where you can smell coffee at six in the morning. Then they add a second detail with which or whose: a street which goes down to the river, a house whose windows are always open. Details like these make a picture in the other person's head. So try it. Choose one place you love, and describe it in three sentences, with three real details. You will see that the listener stops thinking about your English and starts seeing your place.

When I was twenty-five, I lived in a tiny apartment in Chicago whose kitchen was smaller than my car. I couldn't work there, so every morning I walked to a coffee shop on the corner. It was a cozy place where the owner knew everybody's name. The tables were old, the coffee was strong, and there was a big window which looked out on the train station. I wrote my first book at that window, one page a day, for two years. The coffee shop closed last year. People say it was nothing special, but for me it was the most important place in the whole city.

extra_audio.text: First, I choose one place that I really know. Then I start with one small detail, not a big word. After that, I add a second detail with which or whose. Next, I say how the place makes me feel. In the end, I tell the listener why it's worth a visit.

reading.rtitle: Three Underrated Corners of São Paulo
paras: Most visitors see São Paulo as a fast-paced city which never stops: traffic, offices and long lines. That is true, but it is only half of the story. If you go off the beaten path, you find neighborhoods where the city slows down and becomes almost laid-back.

My first favorite is a small square where artists paint the walls every month. It is a vibrant place, full of color and music, and the coffee shops around it are cozy enough for a long conversation on a rainy afternoon.
The second is an old library whose reading room is so spacious and quiet that you forget you are in a city of twelve million people. It is well-connected, too: the metro station is two minutes away.

The third is my aunt's street, which nobody would put in a guidebook. It has a bakery, a tiny park and neighbors who still say good morning. For me, that is the most underrated place of all. -- Marina
